etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English devisen, devysen, from Old French deviser, from Vulgar Latin devisō, from Latin dīvisō, frequentative of dīvidō.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To use one’s intellect to plan or design (something).

quote.citation: c. 1503–1512, John Skelton, Ware the Hauke; republished in John Scattergood, editor, John Skelton: The Complete English Poems, 1983, →OCLC, page 62, lines 20–23:
quote.text: Therefore to make complayntOf such mysadvysedParsons and dysgysed,Thys boke we have devysed,  […]

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act I, scene ii:
quote.text: His fiery eies are fixt vpon the earth.As if he now deuiſ’d some Stratageme:Or meant to pierce Auernus darkſome vauts.To pull the triple headed dog from hell.

quote.citation: 1834–1874, George Bancroft, History of the United States, from the Discovery of the American Continent, volume (please specify |volume=I to X), Boston, Mass.: Little, Brown and Company [et al.], →OCLC:
quote.text: devising schemes to realize his ambitious views

quote.citation: 1988, Andrew Radford, Transformational Grammar, Cambridge: University Press, →ISBN, page 23:
quote.text: Thus, the task of the linguist devising a grammar which models the linguistic competence of the fluent native speaker is to devise a finite set of rules which are capable of specifying how to form, interpret, and pronounce an infinite set of well-formed sentences.

quote.citation: 2019 March 21, Setboonsarg, Chayut, Johnson, Kay, “Numbers game: How Thailand's election system favors pro-army parties”, in Robert Birsel, editor, Reuters‎[1], Reuters, retrieved 2019-03-23:
quote.text: Thailand goes to the polls on Sunday under a new system that critics say the military government has devised to prevent the most popular political party, which has won every election since 2001, from returning to power.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, archaic) To form a scheme; to lay a plan; to contrive; to consider.

quote.citation: 1725, Homer, “Book IX”, in [William Broome], transl., The Odyssey of Homer. […], volume II, London:  […]  Bernard Lintot, →OCLC:
quote.text: I thought, devised, and Pallas heard my prayer.

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic) To plan or scheme for; to plot to obtain.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book VI, Canto IX”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 30:
quote.text: For wisedome is most riches; fooles therefore / They are, which fortunes doe by vowes deuize,

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: I do protest I neuer iniur’d thee, But lou’d thee better then thou can’st deuise: Till thou shalt know the reason of my loue.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French devise. Doublet of device.

definitions.definition: The act of leaving real property in a will.
Such a will, or a clause in such a will.

quote.citation: 1834–1874, George Bancroft, History of the United States, from the Discovery of the American Continent, volume (please specify |volume=I to X), Boston, Mass.: Little, Brown and Company [et al.], →OCLC:
quote.text: Fines upon devises were still exacted.

definitions.definition: The real property left in such a will.

quote.citation: 2010, Carl Anderson, Fragments of a Scattered Brain, →ISBN, page 83:
quote.text: I don't know how I got to be so sour on life, but I'm constantly in solitary confinement of my own devise,  […]
